name: Gangtok & East Sikkim
tagline: A hilltop capital and the old road to Tibet
meta_description: Gangtok and East Sikkim on a fair budget: Rumtek, Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La, the Zuluk Silk Route, permits explained and real 2025–26 costs.
summary: Gangtok, Sikkim's capital at about 1,650 m, sits 114 km above Siliguri. From it, permit roads climb to Tsomgo Lake, Nathu La on the Tibet border and the Silk Route villages of Zuluk and Gnathang, while Rumtek, Aritar and Pakyong lie lower down. A good trip costs ₹2,000–3,500 a day.

story.title: From Lepcha forest to a border state
paras: The first people of these hills were the Lepcha, who call Sikkim Nye-mae-el, and the Bhutia, who came from Tibet and call it Denjong, the valley of rice. In 1642 Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated the first Chogyal at Yuksom, and his dynasty ruled Sikkim for 333 years. For most of that time East Sikkim was a frontier of forest and high grazing grounds, crossed by a handful of passes: Nathu La and Jelep La above the Chumbi valley, where Tibet reaches south between Sikkim and Bhutan.

The British wanted those passes for trade. In 1888 a British force pushed Tibetan troops back from Lingtu and fought them again at Gnathang, and the Anglo-Chinese Convention of 1890 drew the Sikkim–Tibet border along the watershed and made Sikkim a British protectorate. In 1894 Chogyal Thutob Namgyal moved his capital to Gangtok, then a small hamlet on a ridge. Mule trains carried wool, salt and tea through Gangtok, Zuluk and Kupup, and in 1958 Jawaharlal Nehru opened the first motor road from Gangtok towards Nathu La.

Then the border closed. After the 1962 war the passes were sealed, and in September 1967 Indian and Chinese troops fought at Nathu La itself. In 1975 the monarchy ended and Sikkim became India's 22nd state. The high road became an army road, opened to Indian tourists at Nathu La in 1999, and border trade returned through the pass on 6 July 2006. Today East Sikkim lives on that history: soldiers, shrines, homestays on the old trade route, and a capital that grew from a hamlet into a town of about 100,000.

intro: East Sikkim is the most visited part of the state, and almost every trip runs through Gangtok. The town sits on a ridge at about 1,650 m, with the royal chapel and old palace at the top and the car-free MG Marg below. It is a good base for three or four nights: a day for the town's monasteries and the Tibetology museum, a day for Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir, a day for Nathu La, and half a day for Rumtek across the valley.

Beyond Gangtok the land splits in two. To the east, a single army road climbs from rhododendron forest to the bare high country of Tsomgo, Nathu La and Kupup, all above 3,700 m and all on permits. To the south-east, the old trade road climbs from Rangpo and Rongli through Padamchen to Zuluk and Gnathang, the Silk Route of travel brochures, where families run simple homestays. Lower down, Aritar's lake and Pakyong's airport hill are quieter stops.

This land costs a little more than the Darjeeling hills, because the high places can only be reached by registered Sikkim vehicles and every permit trip needs a car or a shared tour seat. Gangtok itself is cheap: dorm beds for ₹500–800, momos and thukpa for under ₹200, shared taxis around town. The way to save is to share: join a shared Tsomgo jeep, split an SUV for the Silk Route, and book homestays directly.
facts: Tsomgo, Nathu La and Silk Route permits; RAP for foreigners

highlights.title: Gangtok on foot
highlights.text: Walk MG Marg, the car-free main street, then climb to Enchey Monastery and drop down to the Do-drul Chorten with its 108 prayer wheels and the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, opened by Nehru in 1958. Momos and thukpa cost under ₹200, and most of the centre is walkable.

highlights.title: Tsomgo Lake at 3,753 m
highlights.text: About 40 km from Gangtok, Tsomgo is a glacial lake about 836 m long, frozen for much of the winter and held sacred by the Sikkimese; monks once read the future in its colours. The road climbs through the Kyongnosla Alpine Sanctuary, red with rhododendrons in April and May.

highlights.title: Nathu La, the border pass
highlights.text: At 4,310 m, Nathu La is where the Gangtok road meets the Tibet border, with only a fence between Indian and Chinese soldiers. Indian citizens may visit on set days with a permit arranged a day ahead in Gangtok; foreigners may not. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Rumtek, the Karmapa's seat
highlights.text: Across the valley from Gangtok, 24 km by road, Rumtek was rebuilt by the 16th Karmapa after he left Tibet in 1959 and inaugurated on Losar in 1966. It is the largest monastery in Sikkim, with a golden stupa holding his relics and a college for monks.

highlights.title: The Silk Route at Zuluk
highlights.text: The old Kalimpong–Lhasa trade road climbs from Rongli through Padamchen to Zuluk, about 2,900 m, where the army road folds into tier after tier of hairpin bends. Family homestays charge about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals. A Silk Route permit from Rongli is needed.

highlights.title: Gnathang and Kupup high country
highlights.text: Above the tree line, the Gnathang valley at about 3,800–4,000 m holds yak herders, a small monastery and the memorials of the 1888 war. A little further, Kupup looks down on Bitang Tso, the Elephant Lake, below the Dongkya Range close to Jelep La.

getting_there: The railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the airport is Bagdogra, both on the edge of Siliguri, about 114–124 km and 4–5 hours below Gangtok. Shared Sikkim-registered jeeps and taxis leave from the SNT stand and the Panitanki More area in Siliguri when full, for about ₹350–500 a seat; Sikkim Nationalised Transport buses cost about ₹250–350 and take five hours or more. A reserved small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹3,500–5,000, an SUV ₹4,500–6,500. The road, NH10, follows the Teesta to Rangpo, the first town in Sikkim. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood it has closed for days at a time, and vehicles then detour via Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock, adding hours. Pakyong airport, 31 km from Gangtok, has had long gaps without scheduled flights. Check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens need no permit to enter Sikkim or Gangtok, but do need permits for Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La, arranged a day ahead through a registered Gangtok tour operator with photo ID and passport photos, and for the Silk Route (Zuluk, Gnathang, Kupup), issued at Rongli. Nathu La is open to Indian nationals only, on set days of the week, usually not Mondays or Tuesdays. Foreigners need a Restricted Area Permit for Sikkim, free at Rangpo or online, and may visit Tsomgo on a Protected Area Permit through a registered agent, usually in groups of two or more; the Silk Route rules for them change often. Check current status before you travel.
money: On a shoestring, ₹1,800–2,500 a day covers a dorm bed or plain room in Gangtok (₹500–1,500), local meals at ₹150–300, shared jeeps and a shared seat on the Tsomgo and Baba Mandir tour (₹800–1,200). A comfortable budget of ₹3,500–5,000 buys a good budget-hotel room, a reserved car for Tsomgo and Nathu La (about ₹5,500–7,500 a car), and two nights on the Silk Route in an SUV shared by four. People overspend in three places: hotel rooms on MG Marg booked late in October or May, reserved cars for trips a shared seat would cover, and package tours that bundle a dozen 'points' in Gangtok. Homestays on the Silk Route, at ₹1,200–2,000 with meals, are the best value in the land.

months.weather: Gangtok 4–13 °C, dry, clear; Tsomgo frozen, snow above 3,500 m
months.summary: Cold, clear and quiet after New Year week. Gangtok has sharp mornings with Kanchenjunga on the skyline, and room rates fall. Tsomgo Lake is usually frozen and snow covers the road to Nathu La, which can close for days after a heavy fall. The Silk Route above Zuluk is often snowbound. It suits travellers who want snow and will accept that permit trips may be cancelled at short notice.
months.tip: Keep a spare day for Tsomgo or Nathu La, since snow closes the road after heavy falls; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Gangtok 5–15 °C, mostly dry, cold nights; snow at Tsomgo and Nathu La
months.summary: Still cold up high, a little milder in Gangtok. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, often falls in February, and Rumtek holds protector dances in the days before it. Tsomgo is usually still frozen. Off-season rates hold, and the town is pleasant to walk. Snow can still close the Nathu La and Silk Route roads, so plan the high trips with slack.
months.tip: Ask at Rumtek for the dates of the Losar dances, which follow the lunar calendar and move each year.

months.summary: Spring arrives. Rhododendrons start to flower at middle heights, the snow pulls back from the Nathu La road, and the Silk Route usually reopens. Losar sometimes falls in early March. Mornings are clearest; afternoons can be hazy. Prices are still moderate until the Holi and Easter holidays, when Bengal families arrive in numbers.
months.tip: Go up to Tsomgo early in the day, before cloud rises from the valleys in the afternoon.

months.summary: One of the best months. The Kyongnosla sanctuary below Tsomgo and the slopes around Zuluk and Gnathang turn red and pink with rhododendrons, the high roads are usually open, and days are long. Tsomgo may still have ice at its edges. Expect occasional evening showers and busier roads towards the end of the month as school holidays begin.
months.tip: Book Silk Route homestays a few weeks ahead for the late April rhododendron season.

months.summary: Peak holiday season. Gangtok is full, hotel rates are at their highest and the Tsomgo and Nathu La roads have long queues of vehicles at checkpoints. In return, everything is open and the high country is green and flowering. Saga Dawa, marking the Buddha's birth, enlightenment and death, can fall in late May or June, with a procession through Gangtok.
months.tip: Book rooms and permit trips early in May, and start for Nathu La at dawn to beat the queues.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives in early to mid June. Views close in, landslides start on NH10 and the Silk Route, and permit trips are cancelled whenever roads slip. Saga Dawa sometimes falls in June. Gangtok itself stays pleasant on dry spells, and rooms get cheaper. We would not plan a first trip for this month.
months.tip: Allow a buffer day before any train or flight, because NH10 can shut at short notice; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Gangtok 17–23 °C, heavy rain, cloud most days
months.summary: The wettest stretch of the year. Landslides close roads for hours or days, and the Teesta runs high along NH10. Tsomgo and Nathu La trips run when the road is clear but often show only cloud. Gangtok's monasteries and museum are quiet and green, and off-season rates are low for those who must travel now.
months.tip: Stay flexible and base yourself in Gangtok, making short trips only when the road reports are clear.

months.summary: Still monsoon, with landslides and mist. Pang Lhabsol, the Sikkimese festival honouring Mount Kanchenjunga as guardian deity, can fall in late August or September, with masked dances at the Tsuklakhang royal chapel. Long-weekend crowds from Bengal arrive around Independence Day. Rumtek and Gangtok are the safest plans.
months.tip: If Pang Lhabsol falls during your stay, reach Tsuklakhang early for a place to watch the dances.

months.weather: Gangtok 15–22 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The monsoon weakens through the month, and by the last week clear mornings return. Pang Lhabsol may fall in early September. Roads are still being repaired after the rains, so expect delays on NH10 and the Silk Route. Prices stay low until the Puja holidays, which bring large numbers of Bengali families in late September or October.
months.tip: Book October Puja week rooms and cars by early September, as Gangtok fills fast.

months.summary: The best month for views. The air is washed clean, Kanchenjunga stands clear most mornings, and the high roads to Tsomgo, Nathu La and Zuluk are open and dry. It is also the busiest month because of the Puja holidays, so rooms and cars cost more and permit queues are long. Book ahead and start early.
months.tip: Sleep at Zuluk for the Lungthung sunrise over Kanchenjunga, at its clearest in October and November.

months.summary: Clear, cool and calmer after the Puja rush. This is our favourite month for the Silk Route: the Kanchenjunga views from Lungthung and Gnathang are reliable and the first snow can dust the high passes late in the month. Nights at Gnathang and Kupup are well below freezing. Rates soften from mid November.
months.tip: Carry a down jacket, gloves and a warm hat for any trip above 3,500 m from November on.

months.weather: Gangtok 5–15 °C, dry, clear; snow at Nathu La
months.summary: Clear and cold, with snow building on the high roads. Losoong, the Sikkimese harvest new year, brings Kagyed masked dances to the monasteries around Gangtok, including Tsuklakhang. Christmas and New Year weeks are busy and expensive, and snow can close Nathu La and the road beyond Tsomgo. Early December is quiet and good value.
months.tip: Travel in the first half of December for clear skies and low rates before the holiday crowds.

faqs.q: How many days do we need for Gangtok and East Sikkim?
faqs.a: Four to five nights covers the main things: two nights in Gangtok for the town and Rumtek, a day each for Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La, and a spare day for weather. Add two or three nights for the Silk Route through Zuluk and Gnathang, which needs its own permit and a car. Six to eight nights in all lets you go slowly.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian citizens need no permit for Gangtok, but Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La each need a permit, arranged through a registered Gangtok tour operator, usually a day in advance, with a photo ID and passport photos. The operator books it with your car or shared seat. Nathu La opens only on set days. Check current status before you travel.

No. Nathu La is open to Indian citizens only. Foreign nationals need a Restricted Area Permit to enter Sikkim, which is free and issued at Rangpo or online, and can visit Tsomgo Lake on a Protected Area Permit through a registered agent, usually as a group of two or more. Rules for foreigners on the Silk Route change often. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which days is Nathu La open?
faqs.a: Nathu La usually opens to tourists on four or five days a week and stays shut on Mondays and Tuesdays, but the days change with army orders, weather and snow, and the road can close without notice after a heavy fall. Ask your Gangtok operator when you apply for the permit a day ahead, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the road from Siliguri to Gangtok open?
faqs.a: Usually, but NH10 along the Teesta has closed often since the October 2023 flood, sometimes for days. When it shuts, jeeps and cars take the longer road via Kalimpong, Pedong and Rhenock, which adds two to three hours. Ask your jeep stand or hotel the day before, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit East Sikkim?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest views and open roads, and early December is clear and quiet. March to May brings rhododendrons and warmer days but bigger crowds in May. December to February brings snow at Tsomgo and Nathu La, which can close roads. June to September is monsoon, with landslides and cloud.

faqs.q: How much does a Gangtok trip cost per person?
faqs.a: Budget about ₹2,000–3,500 per person a day. A dorm or plain room in Gangtok costs ₹500–1,500, a shared Tsomgo and Baba Mandir seat ₹800–1,200, and local meals ₹150–300. A reserved car for Tsomgo and Nathu La costs about ₹5,500–7,500, so it pays to share. Silk Route homestays are ₹1,200–2,000 with meals.

faqs.q: Is Tsomgo Lake or Nathu La safe for children and older people?
faqs.a: Healthy children and older travellers usually manage a short visit, but Tsomgo is at 3,753 m and Nathu La at 4,310 m, and you drive up from 1,650 m in a few hours. Walk slowly, drink water, keep warm and do not stay long at the top. People with heart or lung problems should take medical advice first, and anyone unwell should go down.

faqs.q: Can we drive our own car to Tsomgo or Nathu La?
faqs.a: Generally no. Permits for Tsomgo, Nathu La and the high road beyond are issued with Sikkim-registered tourist vehicles booked through registered operators, so most travellers leave their own car in Gangtok and hire a local taxi or join a shared jeep. Rules for private vehicles change, so ask a registered operator and check current status before you travel.
